No red flags were reported and no rules fired, so the floor is SELF_CARE. Age is unknown, but the first-person wording suggests an adult. Home care with clear return precautions is appropriate. One screening question covers red flags or high-risk status that would change management.
clarifying_questions: Do you have any trouble breathing, drooling or trouble swallowing your own saliva, a muffled voice, or a weakened immune system (for example chemotherapy, transplant, or high-dose steroids)?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW for difficulty breathing, drooling or inability to swallow saliva, a muffled voice, or trouble opening the mouth. - Drooling or inability to swallow.
- A muffled voice.
- A stiff neck.
- Confusion.

- Severe or one-sided throat pain.
- White patches on the tonsils with fever.
- Ear or face pain.

She needs an in-person exam today to judge severity and depth, assess vascular and sensory status, check glucose, and consider culture, X-ray and antibiotics. There is no fever, so nothing reported yet meets emergency criteria. Answers suggesting a severe or limb-threatening infection would escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW.

Have you had chills, shaking, sweating, nausea or vomiting, or felt confused or unusually unwell?
What have your blood sugar readings been over the last day or two? Are they much higher than usual (for example, above 300 mg/dL)?
agent_judgment.escalation_trigger: Escalate to EMERGENCY_NOW if she reports any of the following: spreading redness or red streaks, redness extending well beyond the wound, pus or foul smell, black or dark skin, fever or chills, vomiting, confusion, feeling very unwell, or blood sugars persistently above about 300 mg/dL. agent_judgment.safety_net: Go to the emergency department or call 911 right away if any of these happen: redness spreads quickly or you see red streaks up your leg; pus, a bad smell, or black or dark skin appears; you develop fever, chills, vomiting or confusion; your blood sugars stay very high; or the pain gets much worse.

Active ideation, a plan, intent, access to lethal means or inability to stay safe would escalate this. Minimizing language does not lower urgency.

Do you have access to firearms, stockpiled medications, or other means you might use to hurt yourself?
Is anyone with you right now, or someone you could ask to stay with you today?

agent_judgment.safety_net: If at any point you feel you might act on these thoughts or can't keep yourself safe, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, 24/7) or call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department right away. Thanks for reaching out. A scratchy throat with no fever and no trouble swallowing is most often from a common cold virus, and it usually gets better on its own in a few days to a week. Antibiotics won't help a viral sore throat, but these can make you more comfortable:

- Pain relief: Ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin) 200–400 mg every 6–8 hours with food, OR acetaminophen (Tylenol) 500–1000 mg every 6 hours. Don't exceed 3,000 mg of acetaminophen a day, and follow the package directions.
- Throat lozenges or sprays: Lozenges or numbing sprays with benzocaine or menthol (like Cepacol or Chloraseptic) can soothe the throat.
- Salt-water gargle: Mix 1/2 teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water and gargle a few times a day.
- Honey: Try a spoonful of honey in warm tea or water.
- Fluids and air: Drink plenty of fluids. A humidifier at night can help, and try to avoid smoke or vaping.

Please message us if you get a fever over 101°F, white patches on your tonsils, swollen glands in your neck, a lot of fatigue, a rash, worsening or one-sided throat pain, or if it's not improving after 7–10 days.

Call 911 or go to the ER right away for any of these:
- trouble breathing
- drooling or being unable to swallow your own saliva
- a muffled voice
- trouble opening your mouth
- swelling or stiffness in your neck

Feel better soon!

agent_judgment.patient_reply:
This sounds like typical poison ivy, and it can usually be managed at home. New spots showing up in the same area over the next few days is normal. That happens because skin that got less oil reacts later, not because the blisters are spreading it. Here's what helps:

- Wash your skin with soap and water if you haven't already. Also wash your clothes, gloves, tools, and anything else that touched the plant, since the oil stays on surfaces and can re-expose you.
- Use cool compresses or cool showers, plus calamine lotion, for itch.
- Apply 1% hydrocortisone cream 2–3 times daily. It's mild, so if it isn't enough, let us know.
- Take an oral antihistamine like diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at bedtime to help you sleep. Note that it causes drowsiness, so don't drive after taking it.
- Don't pop the blisters. Keep your nails short to avoid scratching open the skin.
- The rash usually lasts 1–3 weeks.

A few quick questions:
1. Is the rash on your face, near your eyes, on your genitals, or covering large areas beyond your forearms?
2. Any pus, yellow crusting, spreading redness or warmth, red streaks, or increasing pain?
3. Did you burn any of the brush or breathe in the smoke?

If you answer yes to any of these, reply and a physician will review. You may need a prescription steroid.

Call 911 right away if you develop trouble breathing, wheezing, or swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat. Seek care today if you get a fever, pus, red streaks, or swelling around your eyes. Message us if it isn't improving in 7–10 days.

1. Steroid nasal spray. This is the most effective option, especially for a stuffy nose. Options include fluticasone (Flonase), triamcinolone (Nasacort), or budesonide (Rhinocort). Use 1–2 sprays per nostril once daily, aimed slightly away from the center of the nose. It takes a few days to work fully, so use it every day during your allergy season, not just as needed.

2. Non-drowsy antihistamine pill, once daily, for sneezing and itching. Options include cetirizine (Zyrtec), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). Cetirizine can make some people slightly sleepy. Avoid older antihistamines like diphenhydramine (Benadryl), which cause more drowsiness.

- swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat
- eye pain or vision changes

- Keep the same wake-up time every day, including weekends, even after a bad night.
- Use your bed only for sleep. If you can't fall asleep within about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in dim light, then return when you feel sleepy.
- Avoid naps, or keep them under 20 minutes before mid-afternoon.
- Stop caffeine after noon and limit alcohol, which disrupts sleep later in the night.
- Put screens away 30 to 60 minutes before bed, and keep the bedroom cool, dark, and quiet.
- Try a wind-down routine. Some people find it helps to write tomorrow's to-do list or worries on paper earlier in the evening so they're not in your head at bedtime.
- Get daylight and some physical activity earlier in the day.
- Free apps based on CBT for insomnia, such as CBT-i Coach, can be very effective.

To make sure nothing else is contributing, please reply with answers to these:
1. In the past 2 weeks, have you felt down or hopeless, or lost interest in things you enjoy? Have you had any thoughts of being better off dead or of hurting yourself?
2. Has anyone noticed you snoring loudly, stopping breathing, or gasping in your sleep?
3. Any hot flashes, night sweats, or changes in your periods?
4. Any weight loss, racing heart, or shakiness?
5. Have you nearly fallen asleep while driving?
6. How much caffeine and alcohol do you have? Have you started any new medications or supplements?

If you answer yes to any of these, one of our physicians will follow up with you. We may also recommend a visit or some simple tests.

Please don't drive if you feel drowsy. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 or call 911 right away. If your sleep isn't improving after 3 to 4 weeks of these changes, message us and we'll set up a visit.
